title: Effects of visual stimulation using wooden-wall images with different amounts of knots on psychological and physiological responses
research_question: To assess whether knotty wood surface can reduce not only psychological but also physiological benefits for humans, specifically investigating the impact of the presence or absence and the number of knots on physiological and psychological responses.

participants.description: Adult Japanese female university students (mean age 21.7±1.3 years; mean height 157.1±4.5 cm; mean weight 47.5±3.7 kg; mean right eyesight 0.8±0.3; mean left eyesight 0.9±0.2). Excluded individuals with menstrual period, treated for diseases, or who smoke.
participants.recruitment: Recruited and participated in this study to bring the attributes of the participants closer to the previous experiment (Ikei et al. 2020).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three full-sized virtual wooden-wall images (1990x1990 pixels) of Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica) with varying amounts of knots: 'Image with several knots' (66 knots, 0.689% knot ratio), 'Image with few knots' (14 knots, 0.124% knot ratio), and 'Image without knots' (1 knot, 0.003% knot ratio). Images were processed to standardize color and contrast, and all knots were tiny (<20 mm diameter). Displayed on a large LCD monitor (970x970 mm²) for 90s each.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Fig. 1, Table 1, and 'Preparation of wooden-wall images' section

measures.construct: Autonomic nervous system activity (heart rate variability)
measures.instrument: Electrocardiograph (ActivTracer AC-301A) with power spectral analysis (MemCalc/Win) for HF and LF/HF ratio

measures.construct: Mood states (confusion-bewilderment, fatigue-inertia, vigor-activity, friendliness, total mood disturbance)
measures.instrument: Profile of Mood State 2nd Edition (POMS2) brief version

mechanisms: Visual inhomogeneity (knots) in wooden surfaces may affect psychological responses by influencing aesthetic perception and preference.
Cultural appraisal of knotty woods (e.g., traditional values considering knot-free lumber as superior) may influence subjective evaluations.
moderators: Respiratory rate (controlled for in HRV analysis by excluding 4 participants)
implementation_implications: Wooden-wall images, even with some knots, can promote psychological comfort and relaxation.
To maximize psychological benefits, using wooden-wall images with fewer knots is preferable over those with several knots.

The psychological benefits of wooden-wall images with few knots are similar to those without knots, suggesting that a small number of knots may not significantly detract from positive psychological effects.

limitations: The contrast (irregularity of color) of knotty wooden-wall images used in this study might be considerably lower than that of real knotty surfaces, potentially leading to mild visual stimuli and insufficient responsivity of measuring systems for detecting slight physiological changes.
The study only included young women in their twenties, limiting the generalizability of findings to other demographics.

Cultural appraisal of knotty woods (e.g., traditional values) might have affected subjective evaluations, suggesting a need for studies with non-Japanese participants or screened participants based on their likes/dislikes for knotty wood.

paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractWood is an important material used in decorating human living environment. Knots are prominent features found on wood surface. Moreover, they are commonly considered as undesirable surface defects, which reduce not only the mechanical properties but also the aesthetic qualities of lumber. The effects of visual stimulation using knotty wood on psychological responses among humans have been relatively well investigated. However, only few studies have assessed physiological responses. Hence, the present study aimed to assess whether knotty wood surface can reduce not only psychological but also physiological benefits for humans. Two full-sized knotty wooden-wall images and a clear wooden-wall image were used as visual stimuli using computer graphics techniques. Twenty-eight adult Japanese female university students viewed each image for 90 s in random order. During exposure to the visual stimuli, the oxyhemoglobin concentrations in the left and right prefrontal cortex and heart rate variability were consecutively measured and utilized as indicators of central and autonomic nervous system activities, respectively. In addition, the psychological effects of knotty images were examined using the modified semantic differential method and the Profile of Mood State 2nd Edition. There was no significant difference in the effects of the three images on physiological responses. All visual stimuli more or less promoted psychological comfort and relaxation. However, compared with the clear wooden-wall image, the wooden-wall image with several knots was associated with reduced psychological benefits, and the psychological responses in viewing the wooden-wall image with few knots did not remarkably differ.
